newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Petrol price war heats up in South Korea.
newsitem.headline: Petrol price war heats up in South Korea.

text.p: A price war at South Korea's petrol pumps is heating up, analysts said on Monday.
The country's biggest refinery Yukong Ltd threw down the latest gauntlet, slashing prices to the lowest in the market.
Analysts, who had previously expected a price war to be short lived because of the cost to the refiners' bottom line, now say cut-throat competition could continue for some time.
Petrol prices have been falling at South Korean pumps since March, after the government freed prices from central control on January 1.
Yukong, which has the biggest slice of the retail market at 35 percent, had maintained the highest pump prices.
But the refiner unexpectedly slashed the prices on Sunday to the lowest in the land.
"We have lowered our petrol price to dismiss our image as a company that sells the most expensive petrol and to show appreciation to our fixed customers," a company spokesman said.
Yukong dropped retail petrol prices to 823 won (US$92 cents) per litre from 829 won.

Yukong's previous price of 829 won was higher than the 826 won currently charged by Ssangyong Oil Refining Co, Hyundai Oil Refinery Co and Hanwha Energy Co Ltd. LG-Caltex Oil Corp has been selling petrol for 829 won.
The Yukong spokesman said its price cut would hurt other oil companies.
"It's not intentional, but the price cut would deal a severe blow to other oil refiners because we have such a large number of the petrol stations," he said.
It is also the biggest refiner in Asia, with a capacity of 810,000 barrels per day (bpd).
Officials at other refiners said they expected a negative impact from the Yukong's price cut.
"Because Yukong has such a large market share, it could be damaging to other refiners," said a spokesman at LG-Caltex Oil.
Although other refiners have not yet introduced steps to counter the Yukong cut, analysts said the refiners would follow suit just to protect market share.
"Other refiners are likely to drop their prices to the Yukong's level to prevent a loss in market share," said Lee Sang-koo, an energy analyst at Hyundai Securities.
Yukong cut prices because it had lost market share to other refiners who had cut prices during recent months, analysts said.
"Yukong's market share has dropped by one-two percentage points since the beginning of this year," said Lee at Hyundai Securities.
Analysts said a sustained price war was now on the cards.
"A price war is expected to continue for a time being. Maybe for one to two years," said Han Yong, an energy analyst at Jardine Fleming Securities.
Analysts had expected a price war to be short lived because of falling domestic demand for petrol, a slow down in economic growth and poor results in 1996.
Profits of South Korean refiners were savaged last year, largely because of foreign exchange movements.
A round of vicious price cutting in 1994 was sparked by Ssangyong's effort to raise market share. It's share rose at first, but fell back after several months.
